This exercise uses six variables on information and communication technology (ICT), five of them in the clustering, for a different question: can the 55 townships of Shan State, Myanmar, be grouped into a small number of regions, each made of townships with similar access to ICT, and each a single connected piece of territory? Such a grouping is called regionalisation or geographic segmentation. On slide 3, regions are defined as internally homogeneous and contiguous, which combines two requirements: - from cluster analysis, that the townships in a region are similar on the variables; - from spatial analysis, that a region is one connected piece, so that it can be mapped and managed as one area. **Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 12: the data, exploratory analysis, conventional hierarchical clustering, the SKATER and ClustGeo methods of spatially constrained clustering, and the profiles of the clusters. **Part 2** is a review of the chapter's method, with the methods on the Lesson 6 slides that the chapter does not cover: REDCAP, the automatic zoning procedure (AZP) and max-p. A coefficient close to 1 therefore means that most townships are in tight groups, and the groups are joined to each other only much higher in the tree. The UC Business Analytics tutorial, the source of this part of the chapter, calls this a strong clustering structure. A lower coefficient means that the merges are spread through the tree, with no clear gap between groups. The six clusters are in 24 separate pieces of territory. ## SKATER SKATER (Spatial 'K'luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal) was introduced by Assunção et al. (2006). Slides 7 and 8 of the lecture and Assunção et al. (2006, sections 3.3 and 3.4) describe it in four steps: 1. Represent the townships as nodes of a graph, with an edge between every pair of neighbours. 2. Give each edge a cost, the dissimilarity between the two townships it joins. 3. Reduce the graph to a minimum spanning tree: n − 1 edges that connect all n townships at the lowest total cost. 4. Remove edges from the tree. Each removal splits one branch into two, and each piece that remains is a region. At each step SKATER removes the edge whose removal most reduces the within-region sum of squares. Because every region is a connected piece of the tree, and every edge of the tree joins two neighbours, every region is contiguous by construction. ### Neighbour list SKATER can only join townships that share a boundary. The neighbour list records, for each township, the townships that touch it, and these pairs become the edges of the graph in step 1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shan.nb <- poly2nb(shan_sf) summary(shan.nb) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Neighbour list object: Number of regions: 55 Number of nonzero links: 264 Percentage nonzero weights: 8.727273 Average number of links: 4.8 Link number distribution: 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 5 9 7 21 4 3 5 1 5 least connected regions: 3 5 7 9 47 with 2 links 1 most connected region: 8 with 9 links ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} The block uses one function: ```r poly2nb(pl, queen = TRUE) # spdep ``` - `poly2nb()` finds, for each polygon, the polygons that share at least one boundary point with it (Queen contiguity, the default). The result, the minimum spanning tree, is what SKATER cuts into regions in section 3.2.4. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w) dim(shan.mst) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 54 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(shan.mst) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 28 12 78.78999 [2,] 12 49 59.69478 [3,] 28 13 92.79567 [4,] 13 52 110.55197 [5,] 49 35 124.74445 [6,] 35 37 91.65458 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} The block uses one function: ```r mstree(nbw, ini = NULL) # spdep ``` - `shan.w`, from section 3.2.2, is the neighbour list with the cost of each link. `mstree()` returns `shan.mst`, a matrix with one row for each link of the tree: the row numbers of the two townships in `shan_sf`, and the cost of the link. - `mstree()` computes the minimum spanning tree of the weighted graph by Prim's algorithm: start from one node, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects a node already in the tree to a node not yet in it. - The tree has 54 rows, one fewer than the number of townships, because a tree that connects n nodes has n − 1 edges. - With `ini = NULL`, the starting node is chosen at random. The chapter does not set a seed, so its printout starts from node 54 and this one from a different node. ::: ::: callout-note ## What a minimum spanning tree is A spanning tree is a set of links that connects every point, directly or through other points, without any loop, so there is exactly one path between any two points. With $n$ points it always has $n - 1$ links. A graph has many spanning trees, and the minimum spanning tree is the one whose links have the lowest total cost. The figure uses five points and seven links, with the cost on each link: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-50-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: SKATER cuts a tree because a tree has no loops: removing any one link splits it into exactly two connected pieces, so every cut in section 3.2.4 adds one region, and every region is contiguous. The minimum spanning tree is made of the links between the most similar neighbours, so the links left for cutting are between townships that are already alike, and a cut separates the most different parts of a branch. ::: How Prim's algorithm grows the tree is easiest to see on the same five points. The numbers on the lines are edge costs. Starting from A, the candidates at each step are the edges that join a point already in the tree (blue) to a point outside it (dashed), and the cheapest candidate is added (red): ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-51-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: After four steps all five points are joined by four edges, with a total cost of 10. The weight on D1 is the mixing parameter α: - at α = 0, only the variables count, and the result is ordinary Ward clustering; - at α = 1, only geography counts, and the clusters are compact blocks of territory whatever their ICT rates; - in between, a larger α makes the clusters more compact and less homogeneous. The paper calls this a soft contiguity constraint. Townships that are not neighbours may still end up in the same cluster. ### Ward-like clustering without a constraint With α = 0, ClustGeo is ordinary Ward clustering. Running it first gives the starting point that the geographic constraint then changes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat) plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5) rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = 1:6) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-60-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} The block uses one function: ```r hclustgeo(D0, D1 = NULL, alpha = 0, scale = TRUE, wt = NULL) # ClustGeo ``` - With only `D0`, `hclustgeo()` runs Ward-like clustering on that matrix. `D0` must be a `dist` object. - According to Chavent et al. (2018, section 2.2), `hclustgeo()` is a wrapper of `hclust(method = "ward.D")` applied to the squared dissimilarities divided by 2n. The chapter describes it as the same as the `hclust()` call of section 3.1.7. The two produce different trees, because `ward.D` is applied to unsquared distances in section 3.1.7. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6)) shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |> rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.) qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-61-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: The map is as fragmented as the map in section 3.1.12, and the cluster sizes differ from it: 16, 13, 8, 7, 6, 5 here against 20, 13, 7, 6, 5, 4 there. ### Geographic distances and the choice of α ClustGeo needs a second matrix, D1, of geographic dissimilarities, and a value of α. `st_distance()` supplies D1, and `choicealpha()` measures, for each α, how much homogeneity in the ICT rates is given up for how much geographic homogeneity. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf) distmat <- as.dist(dist) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} The block uses two functions: ```r st_distance(x, y) # sf as.dist(m) # stats ``` - `st_distance()` returns the matrix of distances between every pair of features. For polygons, the distance is the shortest distance between their boundaries. For longitude and latitude it is computed on the sphere, in metres. - `as.dist()` converts the square matrix to a `dist` object, as `hclustgeo()` requires. - The chapter names the object `dist`, the same name as the function `dist()`. R still finds the function when it is called, because it looks for a function by that name, but the name is easy to misread. A township and its neighbour touch, so the shortest distance between them is zero. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K = 6, graph = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-63-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-63-2.png){width=864} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} The block uses one function: ```r choicealpha(D0, D1, range.alpha, K, wt = NULL, scale = TRUE, graph = TRUE) # ClustGeo ``` - `choicealpha()` builds the partition into `K` clusters for each α in `range.alpha`, and measures for each partition the proportion of the total pseudo-inertia (a generalised sum of squares) explained in D0 space and in D1 space. `graph = TRUE` draws both, first as the raw proportions, Q, then as proportions of their own maximum, Qnorm. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(cbind(cr$Q, cr$Qnorm), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Q0 Q1 Q0norm Q1norm alpha=0 0.757 0.131 1.000 0.139 alpha=0.1 0.740 0.284 0.978 0.301 alpha=0.2 0.647 0.626 0.855 0.665 alpha=0.3 0.624 0.692 0.825 0.735 alpha=0.4 0.527 0.831 0.697 0.882 alpha=0.5 0.493 0.874 0.652 0.928 alpha=0.6 0.493 0.874 0.652 0.928 alpha=0.7 0.480 0.879 0.635 0.934 alpha=0.8 0.411 0.940 0.543 0.999 alpha=0.9 0.375 0.918 0.496 0.975 alpha=1 0.191 0.941 0.252 1.000 ``` ::: ::: The chapter uses α = 0.2, read from the charts. The table printed above gives the same values. ::: callout-note ## How to read the `choicealpha()` charts Both charts have α on the horizontal axis and one line for each matrix: - The black line, Q0, is the share of the variation in the ICT rates (D0) that the six clusters explain. It is highest at α = 0, where only the rates count, and falls as α rises. - The red dashed line, Q1, is the share of the geographic variation (D1) that the six clusters explain. Each share is one minus the within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities divided by the total, the quantity that `choicealpha()` calls the proportion of explained pseudo-inertia: $$Q = 1 - \frac{\text{within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities}}{\text{total sum of squared dissimilarities}}$$ The share of variation explained in Part 2 is the same quantity, computed on the z-scores. The first chart draws Q0 and Q1 themselves. The second, Qnorm, divides each line by its own maximum, so both lines start from 1 and the two losses can be compared directly. A useful α is one where Q1 has risen a long way while Q0 has fallen only a little. The printed table has the four lines as columns, Q0, Q1, Q0norm and Q1norm, with one row for each α. ::: ### ClustGeo regions With α chosen, the tree is built again from both matrices and cut into six clusters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2) groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6)) shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |> rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.) qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-65-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: The clusters are more compact than at α = 0, and several of them are still split. The mean over townships is computed for each k from 2 to 10. - `NbClust()` computes up to 30 indices for each k and reports the k that scores best on each index. `index = "all"` runs them all. The silhouette width is (b − a) / max(a, b). It is close to 1 when the township is well inside its cluster, close to 0 when it is on the border between two clusters, and negative when it is closer to another cluster than to its own. SKATER cuts the edge whose removal most reduces the within-region sum of squares. A township whose values are far from all of its neighbours' is expensive to keep attached, so cutting it off as a region of one is often the best single cut. Assunção et al. (2006, section 4) met the same outcome in their own case study. Their unrestricted regionalisation of the 96 districts of São Paulo into eight regions left "the north-eastern region" with "one district only", 0.12% of the city's population, beside a region of 36 districts, and they note that "for many applications, this unbalance is not convenient". Their remedy was a restriction on the regions: a minimum population of 500,000 inhabitants, under which region populations ranged from 651,513 to 2,543,743. `spdep::skater()` implements the restriction through its `crit` and `vec.crit` arguments, which its reference page, linked under "All About R", describes as "limits of group size or limits of population size". The question here is which townships become singletons on the standardised variables, and what a minimum size, first in townships and then in households, does to the regions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} skater_z <- function(crit = NULL, vec.crit = NULL, seed = 1234) { set.seed(seed) w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, nbcosts(shan.nb, as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)), style = "B") tree <- mstree(w) if (is.null(crit)) { spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5)$groups } else if (is.null(vec.crit)) { spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5, crit = crit)$groups } else { spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5, crit = crit, vec.crit = vec.crit)$groups } } sk_z <- skater_z() sort(table(sk_z), decreasing = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sk_z 1 2 3 4 5 6 27 17 8 1 1 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} shan_sf$TS.x[sk_z %in% names(which(table(sk_z) == 1))] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Muse" "Tachileik" "Taunggyi" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} - `skater_z()` repeats the three steps of section 3.2 on the z-scores: edge costs, minimum spanning tree, and SKATER. It returns the region of each township. `crit`, if given, is passed to `spdep::skater()` as a minimum per region. Without `vec.crit` the minimum counts townships; with `vec.crit`, a value for each township, the minimum applies to the sum of those values over the region. - `names(which(table(sk_z) == 1))` finds the regions with one township, and the last line prints the names of those townships. ::: On the standardised variables, three of the six regions are single townships: Muse, Tachileik and Taunggyi. The singletons are the extremes on the variables with almost no weight before standardising (section 4.2). Their z-scores on computer ownership are the three highest in the state (3.3, 3.3, 2.8). Taunggyi is the state capital, and Muse and Tachileik are the main border crossings to China and Thailand. The remaining 52 townships are divided into three large regions. Chavent et al. (2018) illustrate two kinds of D1: geographic distances between the municipalities (section 4.3), and a neighbourhood matrix D1 = 1 − A, where A is the adjacency matrix with 1 on its diagonal (section 4.4). The ClustGeo introduction page, linked under "All About R", specifies the first as "the distances between the town halls of the 303 municipalities", that is, between points. The chapter's matrix measures the distance between polygon boundaries, a third kind. Two of the references use both kinds of D1 on one data set. Jaya et al. (2019) cluster diarrhoea risk in the 30 districts of Bandung with a distance-based and a contiguity-based D1, and prefer the distance-based one because diarrhoea may spread "not limited to adjacent locations but also possible in locations that are far apart". De Souza and Taconeli (2022) run both versions on 399 Paraná municipalities, choose α separately for each (0.25 for distances and 0.15 for neighbourhoods), and find that the neighbourhood version separates the clusters more on the educational indicators. In Jaya et al. and in de Souza and Taconeli, the choice of D1 is a decision about what "near" should mean for the phenomenon, made before α is chosen. The question here is what the chapter's D1 measures, and whether the two matrices from the paper give more contiguous clusters at a smaller loss of homogeneity. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} A <- nb2mat(shan.nb, style = "B") D1_poly <- as.matrix(distmat) off_diag <- row(A) != col(A) tibble(pairs_at_zero = sum(D1_poly[off_diag] == 0) / 2, neighbour_pairs = sum(A) / 2, zero_iff_neighbour = all((D1_poly == 0 & off_diag) == (A == 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 pairs_at_zero neighbour_pairs zero_iff_neighbour 1 132 132 TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} - `nb2mat(style = "B")` converts the neighbour list to a 55 × 55 matrix with 1 for neighbours and 0 otherwise. - `off_diag` is true everywhere except the diagonal. Pairs are counted in both directions in a full matrix, so each count is divided by 2. - The last value tests whether a pair has zero distance exactly when the two townships are neighbours. ::: The pairs with D1 = 0 are exactly the 132 neighbouring pairs. Under this D1, a township is at the same distance, zero, from all of its neighbours, however large they are. Between townships that do not touch, the distance is the gap between their nearest edges, so a long, thin township counts as close to many others. The two alternatives from the paper are built below. Centroid distances need a projected CRS, and Shan State is within UTM zone 47N (96°E to 102°E), EPSG:32647. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shan_utm <- st_transform(shan_sf, 32647) D1_centroid <- as.dist(st_distance(st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_utm)))) A1 <- A diag(A1) <- 1 D1_neighbour <- as.dist(1 - A1) D0_z <- dist(shan_ict.z) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"} - `st_transform(shan_sf, 32647)` projects the layer to UTM zone 47N, in metres. `st_centroid()` then finds the centre of each township on the flat plane, and `st_distance()` between the centroids gives straight-line distances in metres. - `D1_neighbour` follows section 4.4 of Chavent et al. (2018): the adjacency matrix with 1 on the diagonal, subtracted from 1. Neighbours are at dissimilarity 0 and all other pairs at 1. - `D0_z` is the distance matrix on z-scores, used for all three versions of D1 so that only D1 changes. ::: ::: callout-note ## What each D1 measures, for one township The three maps show the dissimilarity between Taunggyi and every other township under each version of D1: - **Polygon distance (chapter):** every neighbour is at 0, however far its centre lies. - **Centroid distance:** dissimilarity grows smoothly with distance. - **Neighbourhood matrix, 1 − A:** neighbours are at 0, and every other township is at 1. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-91-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: Taunggyi is outlined in red. The answer on this page is yes, with qualifications that the chapter does not raise. **The regions depend on the scale of the variables.** On the raw rates, mobile phone and TV make up 81% of the distance, so the chapter's clusters group the townships mainly on those two. After standardising, the SKATER singletons change from Ywangan and Narphan to Taunggyi, Muse and Tachileik. **The number of regions is not settled by the data.** The gap statistic, the silhouette width and NbClust all give fewer than six clusters, and the silhouette widths show weak structure at every k. The merge heights of the Ward tree jump at two, four and six clusters. I would report the six regions as one level of a nested partition, with the two- and four-region levels beside it. **Most of the rates have no spatial pattern.** De Souza and Taconeli (2022) found every one of their indicators spatially autocorrelated; here only radio and land line are. TV and mobile phone, which carry most of the weight in the chapter's clusters, have no significant pattern. That explains the fragmented map of section 3.1.12 better than the omission of location from the method, and it is why contiguity costs about a quarter of the explained variation in section 4.8. **SKATER is not the strongest method on these data.** Before section 4.8, I expected SKATER to be the natural choice, because it is contiguous by construction and taught first. REDCAP full-order and AZP explain more, consistent with the SKATER limitation on slide 9, and without a minimum size three of SKATER's six regions are single townships. Assunção et al. (2006) met the same problem in São Paulo and set a minimum population; here a minimum of 100,000 households gives six regions of 7 to 12 townships. They also found SKATER better than AZP on every data set they tried. On Shan the order is reversed, which fits their own remark that performance "is dependent on the characteristics of the data set". Three calls in the chapter ran without error and without the effect that the text around them describes: - the standardised versions of the data were computed and not used for clustering; - `hclust(method = "ward.D")` was run where the agglomerative coefficient that justified it belongs to `ward.D2`; - `st_distance()` between polygons gave a geographic matrix in which all neighbours are at distance zero. As in chapters 9 and 10, one object is computed and a different object is passed to the next step. All three faults are explained in the course's own sources. The UC Business Analytics tutorial, the source of chapter sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10, standardises with `scale()` and uses `ward.D2`, and Chavent et al. (2018) describe what `hclustgeo()` computes and offer the neighbourhood matrix as D1. **Limits.** Population is not weighted in most of the methods: apart from max-p and the household minimum in section 4.5, a township of 3,318 households counts as much as Taunggyi with 82,604. The weights argument of `hclustgeo()` (Chavent et al., 2018, section 2.2) could give households a weight in ClustGeo.
